Official wording requiring qualification: the event overview loosely mentions derived invocation, while its dedicated guide requires a base raising method; async simplifies suspension to the first await, while await documents immediate continuation for completed operands; filter prose conflicts with the explicit bare-rethrow section and exception best practices; interface summaries overstate static virtual implementation requirements and default-member inheritance, while dedicated pages clarify them. cards.statement: Assigning an ordinary struct to another variable copies the struct's stored value.
cards.explanation: Struct assignment copies the value. Changing an int field in the destination leaves the source's field unchanged.

cards.statement: Assigning a class instance reference to another variable makes both variables refer to that instance.
cards.explanation: Class assignment copies the object reference, so both variables initially reach the same object.

cards.statement: Changing an int parameter passed by value changes the caller's int variable.
cards.explanation: A by-value int parameter holds a copy. Assigning the parameter changes that copy.
cards.misconception: A value parameter aliases the caller's value variable.

cards.statement: Assigning a new object to a by-value class parameter redirects the caller's variable to that object.
cards.explanation: Replacing a by-value class parameter changes its local reference. Mutating the referenced object instead affects the shared instance.
cards.misconception: Replacing a copied reference changes the caller's reference.

cards.statement: Boxing an int stores a copy of its value in the resulting object.
cards.explanation: The boxed value is separate from the original int variable. Later assignments to that variable leave the boxed value unchanged.

cards.statement: For object box = 7, the cast (long)box produces a long containing 7.
cards.explanation: The object holds a boxed int. Unboxing it directly as long throws InvalidCastException; unbox as int before numeric conversion.
cards.misconception: Unboxing performs numeric widening conversions.

cards.statement: Casting a null object reference to int produces the default int value.
cards.explanation: Unboxing a null reference to int throws NullReferenceException.
cards.misconception: Unboxing null supplies the target value type's default.

cards.statement: For string s = "a", s += "x" leaves the original string object's characters intact.
cards.explanation: String objects are immutable. Concatenation assigns the combined content rather than editing the original string object's characters.

cards.statement: For string operands, a == b checks whether both variables refer to the same string object.
cards.explanation: String == compares text content. Equal text can reside in distinct string instances.
cards.misconception: String equality establishes reference identity.

cards.statement: The compiler fixes a var local's type from its initializer at compile time.
cards.explanation: A var local is strongly typed. Later assignments still need to be compatible with the inferred type.

cards.statement: The declaration var item = null gives item the compile-time type object.
cards.explanation: An untyped null literal gives var no type to infer, so var item = null produces a compiler error.
cards.misconception: The compiler infers object from an untyped null literal.

cards.statement: The compiler requires definite assignment before code reads a local int's value.
cards.explanation: Local variables need definite assignment before a read. Class fields receive default values, such as zero for int.

cards.statement: An ordinary struct can inherit from another ordinary struct.
cards.explanation: C# rejects a struct declaration that derives from another struct.
cards.misconception: Structs support struct inheritance.

cards.statement: A readonly struct can hold a List<T> whose contents change after construction.
cards.explanation: A readonly struct protects its own state; a referenced List<T> remains mutable.

cards.statement: default(S) uses zero-initialized fields when S declares a parameterless struct constructor.
cards.explanation: default(S) initializes fields to their defaults instead of calling S's declared parameterless constructor. Struct array elements follow that rule.

cards.statement: The compiler rejects a lambda that captures a ref struct local.
cards.explanation: Capturing a ref struct local in a lambda violates the restrictions on its lifetime.

cards.statement: A ref struct value supports conversion to object through boxing.
cards.explanation: Boxing a ref struct value to object produces a compiler error.
cards.misconception: Ref structs use ordinary struct boxing.

cards.statement: Declaring record Person(string Name) makes Person a reference type.
cards.explanation: The record spelling selects a record class; record struct selects a value type.

cards.statement: A positional record struct restricts synthesized property assignments to initialization.
cards.explanation: Positional record structs synthesize get/set properties; record classes and readonly record structs synthesize get/init properties.
cards.misconception: Positional record struct properties use init.

cards.statement: For record R(int X), new R(3) == new R(3) evaluates to true.
cards.explanation: For record R(int X), the compiler supplies equality that compares the int member's value.

cards.statement: Synthesized record equality compares array members by their element contents.
cards.explanation: Record equality uses each member's equality semantics. Array members compare by reference.
cards.misconception: Record equality recursively compares arrays.

cards.statement: Synthesized record-class equality includes the objects' runtime types in its comparison.
cards.explanation: Record-class equality requires matching runtime types, even when variables share a base record type.

cards.statement: A record class with public set accessors rejects property changes after construction.
cards.explanation: A public set accessor permits a record property's value to change after construction.
cards.misconception: Record classes enforce immutable properties.

cards.statement: The synthesized copy for a record with expression recursively clones referenced child objects.
cards.explanation: The synthesized with copy is shallow: unchanged reference members still point to the same objects.
cards.misconception: Record with copies clone child objects.

cards.statement: A local declared as int? uses the System.Nullable<int> value type.
cards.explanation: The ? suffix on a value type denotes Nullable<T>, which represents a value or an absent value.

cards.statement: Reading Nullable<int>.Value when its HasValue property is false returns zero.
cards.explanation: Nullable<T>.Value throws InvalidOperationException when HasValue is false.
cards.misconception: An empty nullable value returns the underlying type's default through Value.

cards.statement: Assigning null to a string local automatically triggers a runtime null check.
cards.explanation: Assigning null to a non-nullable string local produces a nullable warning. The annotation adds no runtime check.
cards.misconception: A non-nullable reference annotation enforces runtime validation.

cards.statement: Nullable annotations and nullable warnings have separately configurable compiler contexts.
cards.explanation: C# has an annotation context and a warning context. Directives or project settings control them independently.

cards.statement: A null check can change a local's compiler null-state while its string? annotation stays in place.
cards.explanation: Flow analysis tracks whether a value might be null at a particular point. A nullable annotation still permits assigning null later.

cards.statement: Postfix ! can throw immediately when its operand evaluates to null.
cards.explanation: The null-forgiving operator changes compiler analysis. At runtime, x! evaluates to x, including when x is null.
cards.misconception: Postfix ! performs a runtime assertion against null.

cards.statement: For a non-null left operand, ?? skips evaluation of its right operand.
cards.explanation: The ?? operator returns a present left value directly. A fallback call on the right is evaluated when the left value is null.

cards.statement: After string? x = null, executing x ??= "ready" leaves the variable x equal to null.
cards.explanation: When x starts null, x ??= "ready" assigns "ready" to x. The operator performs assignment rather than just returning a fallback.
cards.misconception: Null-coalescing assignment merely supplies a fallback result.

cards.statement: For an int[]? array a, the expression a?[0] has the compile-time type int?.
cards.explanation: Conditional element access lifts an int result to int?. A null array receiver yields null instead of accessing an element.

cards.statement: In C# 14, person?.Name = GetName() evaluates GetName() when person is null.
cards.explanation: A C# 14 null-conditional assignment skips the right-hand expression when its receiver is null.
cards.misconception: Null-conditional assignment evaluates the value even when it skips the setter.

cards.statement: The declaration string[]? names marks the array's string elements as nullable.
cards.explanation: The ? after [] annotates the array reference. Use string?[] to annotate its elements as nullable.
cards.misconception: An array's nullable annotation applies to its elements.

cards.statement: The expression new string[3] creates an array whose elements initially contain null.
cards.explanation: Array allocation initializes reference-type elements to null, even when their element annotation is non-nullable.

cards.statement: The compiler automatically creates a hidden field for an auto-property with get and set accessors.
cards.explanation: The compiler supplies an auto-property's storage and accessor implementations.

cards.statement: A property declared as int Total => Price * Quantity caches its first result for later reads.
cards.explanation: An expression-bodied getter evaluates its expression on each read.
cards.misconception: Computed getters cache their results.

cards.statement: A public property's private set accessor lets its declaring class assign it after construction.
cards.explanation: A private setter remains callable inside the declaring class after the object is initialized.

cards.statement: An init accessor requires a caller to assign the property in an object initializer.
cards.explanation: An init accessor restricts assignment timing; callers can leave the property at its default value.
cards.misconception: An init accessor enforces initialization.

cards.statement: Assigning null to a required string property produces a compiler error.
cards.explanation: Assigning null satisfies a required property's initialization obligation. A non-nullable string property still produces a nullable warning.
cards.misconception: Required properties reject null at compilation.

cards.statement: In C# 14, field in a property accessor accesses the compiler's synthesized backing storage.
cards.explanation: The field keyword lets an accessor use the property's backing field for logic such as validation.

cards.statement: An object initializer assigns its members after the selected constructor runs.
cards.explanation: Object creation executes the constructor before applying the object initializer's member assignments.

cards.statement: In C# 12, an ordinary class's primary-constructor parameters become public properties.
cards.explanation: Ordinary class and struct primary-constructor parameters remain parameters, rather than public properties.
cards.misconception: Primary constructors synthesize public properties.

cards.statement: In C# 12, a primary-constructor parameter is in scope in an instance method of its ordinary class.
cards.explanation: The parameter's scope extends through the type body, including instance member bodies.

source.title: Declare primary constructors for classes and structs

cards.statement: In C# 12, the compiler stores an unused primary-constructor parameter in a hidden instance field.
cards.explanation: The compiler generates parameter storage when a member body accesses that primary-constructor parameter.
cards.misconception: Unused primary parameters receive instance storage.

source.title: Declare primary constructors for classes and structs

cards.statement: In C# 12, a second constructor can bypass its class's primary constructor with a base(...) initializer.
cards.explanation: An additional class constructor chains through this(...), directly or indirectly, to the primary constructor.
cards.misconception: Secondary constructors bypass primary construction.

source.title: Declare primary constructors for classes and structs

cards.statement: In C# 12, a derived primary constructor can pass its parameters to the base-class constructor.
cards.explanation: The derived type's base-type argument list supplies values to the chosen base constructor.
